articles.title: GitHub’s model for secret detection: Finding more secrets with less noise
articles.excerpt: GitHub’s context-aware secret classifier improves detection quality, raises weighted acceptance by 11.5%, and reduces median scan execution time by 86%. The post GitHub’s model for secret detection: Finding more secrets with less noise appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
details: JavaScript draws the arrows connecting these cards. OUR PIPELINE VS. THE PREVIOUS LLM PIPELINE Smarter secret scanning, at a fraction of the cost 11.5% higher acceptance Owner-weighted alert precision 86% lower median scan execution time Post-push scanning 98% lower serving cost Compact model vs. remote LLM calls

Secret scanning works best when developers are confident in the findings. Catch too little, and real credentials can remain in a repository. Alert too often, and developers may spend time investigating strings that aren't secrets.

Generic secrets make that balance especially difficult. The same string could be a real credential or a documentation placeholder, so detecting it requires understanding the surrounding code and text.

To address this challenge, we trained a secret classifier specifically for GitHub's product needs: distinguishing real credentials from lookalikes while meeting the speed and efficiency requirements of scanning at scale.

In our companion post, Secret protection must scale with software , we explained why secret protection must keep pace with AI-accelerated development. Here, we go behind the scenes of the context-aware classifier powering that effort: how we designed, trained, and evaluated it to find more real secrets with less noise.

articles.title: GitHub Copilot app for Beginners: How to teach Copilot about your codebase
articles.excerpt: Learn how to add custom instructions and skills to your repository, use custom agents, and connect MCP servers like Playwright. The post GitHub Copilot app for Beginners: How to teach Copilot about your codebase appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
details: Context matters when you're working with AI. Every codebase has its own house rules: how components are structured, which scripts to run, and which conventions apply to different frameworks and file types.

Copilot can help you make changes across a project, but it works best when it knows those rules, too. Much of that knowledge can live inside the repository, so Copilot can pick it up automatically instead of requiring you to explain the same standards, scripts, and workflows every time you start a new task.
In this installment of our GitHub Copilot app for Beginners series, we'll look at four ways to tailor how Copilot works with your project:
Custom instructions communicate the conventions Copilot should follow.
Custom agents bring specialized guidance to larger tasks.

articles.title: Higgsfield takes AI video from 1 minute to over 10
articles.excerpt: Higgsfield brings creators longer videos with GPT-6 Astra, precise visuals with GPT-Image-2.5, and a path to voice filmmaking with GPT-Live.
details: Higgsfield AI is on a mission to make professional video and image creation accessible to anyone with an idea.
Before GPT‑6 Astra, those videos topped out at around one minute.
Now, says CEO and co-founder Alex Mashrabov, users can create videos over 10 minutes long.
Longer videos are just one way Higgsfield AI helps smaller creative teams take on more ambitious work.
With GPT‑6 Astra, those agents can also call external tools to handle complex, manual work in 3D modeling.

articles.title: What's New in WebGPU (Chrome 155-156)
articles.excerpt: WGSL fragment_depth extension, texture compression unaligned, srgb-linear and display-p3-linear color spaces, snorm10-10-10-2 vertex format, and more.
details: WGSL fragment_depth extension In geometry-intensive render passes, early-Z optimizations are developers' best friend.
They provide a massive performance boost by letting the GPU discard hidden pixels before running expensive fragment shaders.
If a rasterized depth fails the depth test, the GPU skips the fragment shader entirely, provided the shader doesn't have other side effects.
If you want to read into how hardware handles this, MJP has an excellent write-up on When Does Early-Z Have to be Disabled?.
While custom depth manipulation is useful, doing it in your fragment shader comes with a hidden tax.

articles.title: Under the hood, off the hot path: How D1 scales to millions of databases
articles.excerpt: A deep dive into how D1 architected its control plane to scale and manage millions of databases, while keeping data plane query operations at the edge. We share guiding principles on how to build on the Developer Platform effectively.
details: Traditional database architecture assumes you have one or two big database clusters per application, usually accompanied by a connection pooling solution. AI-assisted development and vibe coding platforms turn this model inside out and are driving applications toward many small databases: one per user, application, preview environment, or tenant.
That model fits D1 particularly well. D1 is Cloudflare's managed, serverless database based on SQLite. It allows you to create millions of databases and only pay for what you use.
The question becomes: how do you scale the control plane for millions of databases without making every query slower by sending it through centralized bottlenecks?
We made a lot of architectural changes to scale out D1 to support platforms with millions of created databases, hundreds of thousands of which are active at any point.

This post is a behind-the-scenes deep dive into how the D1 control plane works. Many of the architectural patterns we will describe can be used by anyone building on top of Cloudflare’s Developer Platform. The post also gives a glimpse into how we build our own control planes.

articles.title: Rewinding the exponential: How we keep hardware usage down
articles.excerpt: Our strategies to optimize our data pipeline throughput without compromising data quality.
details: More than 20% of the web sits behind Cloudflare’s network, and our team, the Data team, owns the data pipeline responsible for plumbing that data (and more) from our global network to applicable central data centers.
The Cloudflare network is a globally distributed system supporting tens of thousands of servers.
Data that power Cloudflare Logs , SQL API , observability , internal analytics, and more flow through this network and use our data pipeline to serve customers.
In May of this year, we were providing data delivery at roughly two billion events per second.
This includes customer traffic as well as data sent from internal teams.

articles.title: Filter, reshape, and redact logs before export with Transformers
articles.excerpt: Logpush now supports Transformers, allowing teams to filter, redact, and reshape log streams using SQL before export. Powered by Apache DataFusion and Apache Arrow, Transformers apply those changes directly to log data before it reaches the destination.
details: Logpush delivers logs in batches as quickly as possible, enabling Cloudflare to provide information almost in real time. During our recent Birthday Week , we made Logpush available on all self-serve plans and Transformers generally available.
Those changes were among eight major updates to Cloudflare Observability and reflect our commitment to make every Cloudflare feature available to everyone .
This post takes a deeper look at how Transformers work inside Logpush's export pipeline.
Observability teams use Logpush to export Cloudflare logs to security information and event management systems (SIEMs), analytics platforms, and object storage.
Before those logs reach their destination, teams may need to remove health checks, omit sensitive fields, or reshape records for dashboards and investigations.

articles.title: Docker Hub security advisory: personal access tokens transferred during account-to-organization conversions
articles.excerpt: CVE-2026-105445: Docker Hub account conversion could re-assign personal access tokens to a new owner. Read what happened, who was affected, and the fix.
details: On September 30, 2026, security researchers reported a vulnerability in Docker Hub’s identity and access management through our Vulnerability Disclosure Program.
We confirmed the report and deployed a fix to production the same afternoon, less than four hours after receiving it.

We then reviewed every account conversion back to the date the flaw was introduced, and on October 2, notified every user and organization owner whose account could have been impacted by this vulnerability.
This post explains what the vulnerability was, what it could and could not do, what we found, and what we have changed.

We want to thank Peter Molnar and Krisztian Hozak of mptrdev.com for finding the issue, reporting it responsibly, and coordinating disclosure with us. Their technical write-up is available at ghostpat.com . This issue is tracked as CVE-2026-105445.

articles.title: How one bug bounty researcher chooses the features they investigate
articles.excerpt: As we kick off Cybersecurity Awareness Month, the GitHub Bug Bounty team spotlights @vaib25vicky, exploring their methodology, techniques, and experiences hacking on GitHub. The post How one bug bounty researcher chooses the features they investigate appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
details: As we kick off Cybersecurity Awareness Month, the GitHub Bug Bounty team is excited to spotlight one of the top-performing security researchers participating in the GitHub Security Bug Bounty Program: @vaib25vicky!
The security research community makes GitHub safer for everyone-that's the simple idea behind GitHub's Bug Bounty Program .

For more than a decade, researchers from around the world have helped us identify and fix vulnerabilities before they could be exploited, helping protect the code that powers millions of development projects.

As AI-powered experiences such as GitHub Copilot and the Copilot coding agent reshape how software is built, partnering with skilled researchers across both traditional and emerging attack surfaces matters more than ever.

This year marked a new chapter for our program . We restructured our bounty tables around a core shift in what we incentivize: you don't earn more by submitting more-you earn more by submitting better. As part of this change, we formalized a permanent, invite-only VIP program for researchers who consistently deliver high-quality, high-impact work.

articles.title: Building an evidence-grounded agentic security operations harness on Cloudflare
articles.excerpt: Cloudflare Managed Defense uses a team of specialized AI agents built on Workers and global network telemetry to analyze security alerts. By separating deterministic evidence collection from model inference, the system delivers grounded recommendations to Managed Defense Analysts.
details: Security alerts rarely arrive one at a time. A single alert can cause a spike across the environment, requiring a human analyst to decide which alerts are related and what they mean. When multiple arrive at the same time, it can quickly overwhelm even a seasoned security analyst. Enter the alert paradox. Now, our built-in, multi-AI-agent security operations harness can handle more of this work at Cloudflare scale.
Our Cloudflare Managed Defense AI agent harness speeds up the process of gathering data, connecting and aggregating detections, and accounting for missing sources while new alerts continue to arrive.
To further analyze context, we make use of the OpenAI Daybreak Defense Network and our partnership with Anthropic.
Cloudflare uses approved OpenAI Daybreak and Anthropic models, including GPT-5.6 Cyber and Mythos, for deeper model-backed analysis.
Initial analysis and scoring is done with Clef , Cloudflare’s open-source decision model.

articles.title: Hack the World: Why hackathons are still the best place to learn to build
articles.excerpt: The barriers to building software have collapsed. Today, anyone can build. Hackathons are a great place to start learning. The post Hack the World: Why hackathons are still the best place to learn to build appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
details: Someone bursts through the door and announces, "There's pizza!" Nearby, a team has duct tape and cardboard holding its prototype together. Another is debugging a model that won't detect their movements.
This is a common scene during hackathons, and for a lot of people they're the place to learn to build.
During several recent hackathons, we followed dozens of participants from the badge line to final demos and asked them what keeps them coming back.
Teams come up with ideas for robots, apps, websites, hardware, and more, then try to get prototypes working before time runs out.
These aren't small things, these are big endeavors, and they're going to try to do it in basically two days.

articles.title: Secret protection must scale with software
articles.excerpt: Developers aren’t becoming more careless; they’re being outpaced. The tools that let developers create more software should also take on more of the work of protecting it. The post Secret protection must scale with software appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
details: Today, one in three pull requests on GitHub involves an AI agent . A year ago, that number was fewer than one in 10. If that pace holds, within the next two years, most of the code pushed to GitHub could be written by an agent. Much of it may never be fully read by a human.

If developers and agents move faster, we have a responsibility to ensure protection keeps up with the accelerated rate of code creation. That means preventing more leaks before they happen and making the response to exposures that remain less dependent on manual human effort.

This is a pivotal point for leaked secrets. Developers aren't becoming more careless; they're being outpaced. The tools that let developers create more software should also take on more of the work of protecting it.

In this essay, I share the nine quarters of data behind that claim. I also introduce the fine-tuned classifier we built with Microsoft Applied Sciences to extend push protection to unstructured secrets. The model assesses a whole set of candidate secrets in less than two milliseconds and could more than double the number of secrets that we can prevent.
A new secret appears in publicly visible code about once every two seconds, doubling yearly for the past three years. Public discourse is quick to jump to the idea that AI made developers careless.
